paragraphs: This paper adapts BFGS and its limited-memory version, LBFGS, to convex optimization problems whose objectives are not smooth. These problems can contain corners where an ordinary gradient is insufficient to describe how the objective changes. The goal is to retain the usefulness of these established optimization methods while giving their treatment of nonsmooth objectives a rigorous foundation.

The authors generalize three connected ingredients using subdifferentials, which describe possible slopes at nonsmooth points. These ingredients are the local quadratic approximation, the procedure for finding a direction that decreases the objective, and the Wolfe conditions used to choose a step along that direction. Addressing all three makes the extension a coordinated optimization method.

They apply the resulting sub(L)BFGS algorithm to L2-regularized learning with binary hinge loss. They also apply its direction-finding component to L1-regularized learning with logistic loss. In both settings, the generic methods perform comparably to or better than corresponding components of specialized leading solvers. The results support the practical value of a broadly applicable nonsmooth optimization approach.
icml-2008-a-quasi-newton-approach-to-non.tldr: The paper extends BFGS to nonsmooth convex objectives and reports competitive performance against specialized solvers in two learning settings.

paragraphs: Learning preferences from observations can leave several lexicographic preference models consistent with the available evidence. Earlier approaches select a single model as their best guess. This paper instead retains a collection of consistent models and combines their votes to approximate the target preference model. The central idea is to make predictions using the remaining alternatives collectively.

The authors develop two versions of this approach, called variable voting and model voting. Both implement the broader strategy of avoiding an early commitment to one consistent explanation. They also introduce a learning bias that removes some possible models from consideration. This bias can be used with either voting method, shaping which possibilities contribute to the prediction.

In the reported experiments, the voting methods outperform existing approaches. Adding the learning bias significantly improves the learning curve, particularly when observations are scarce. That finding matters because limited evidence is precisely when several models can remain plausible. The empirical results support combining consistent models and selectively narrowing that collection, without establishing that every voting scheme or pruning rule will improve preference learning.
icml-2008-democratic-approximation-of-le.tldr: Voting across consistent preference models improves empirical learning performance, especially when combined with a bias that prunes possible models.

paragraphs: This paper develops a more efficient algorithm for multiclass maximum margin clustering. Its focus is the optimization needed to obtain a clustering under the maximum margin formulation. The practical motivation is scalability: if solving that formulation takes too long, the size of datasets that can be handled becomes restricted.

The proposed cutting plane algorithm works through a nested sequence of relaxed optimization problems. Each successive relaxation more tightly represents the original clustering problem. This creates a progression of intermediate problems rather than requiring the full formulation to be handled at once. Each problem in that sequence can be solved efficiently using the constrained concave-convex procedure, or CCCP.

Evaluations on several real-world datasets show much faster convergence than existing maximum margin clustering methods, with guaranteed accuracy as described in the abstract. The resulting efficiency allows the algorithm to handle substantially larger datasets. The contribution therefore connects an optimization strategy to a practical gain in scale: progressively tightening the problem makes this clustering approach more computationally accessible.
icml-2008-efficient-multiclass-maximum-m.tldr: A cutting plane method makes multiclass maximum margin clustering faster by solving a sequence of progressively tighter relaxations.

paragraphs: Exponential Family Predictive State Representations describe a stochastic dynamical system through a distribution over a short window of future observations. The parameters of that distribution serve as the state. This representation is attractive for learning because maximum-likelihood expressions do not require hidden quantities, while the model family can capture POMDPs, linear dynamical systems, and additional models.

The computational obstacle is that existing algorithms based on exact likelihood are not feasible to run efficiently. This paper introduces a learning algorithm built around an approximate likelihood. The change makes learning computationally efficient while preserving the predictive-state formulation as the underlying way of representing the system.

The algorithm also has a useful interpretation: it attempts to produce stationary distributions of observations, features, and states that match their empirical counterparts. In plain terms, it seeks agreement between the model's stable statistical behavior and the patterns observed in data. The authors suggest that both the approximate likelihood and this distribution-matching idea may be useful in other model families.
icml-2008-efficiently-learning-linear-li.tldr: An approximate-likelihood algorithm makes learning exponential-family predictive state models computationally efficient.

paragraphs: Expectation-maximization, or EM, is widely used to fit Gaussian mixture models, but it is generally not guaranteed to find the global optimum. Different initial configurations can lead to substantially different local optima. A common response is to run EM several times and retain the best result, which makes the cost of unsuccessful runs an important concern.

This paper proposes estimating an upper bound on the log likelihood that a run's local optimum can achieve, using its current configuration after an EM iteration. The method first bounds the region in which that optimum may lie. It then uses this region to estimate an upper bound on the achievable likelihood.

A run can be stopped when this bound establishes that its eventual result is worse than the best solution already found. The method therefore saves work by identifying runs that cannot improve the current answer. Extensive experiments report effective and efficient acceleration of conventional EM. This improves the multiple-run procedure without claiming to eliminate EM's underlying susceptibility to local optima.
icml-2008-estimating-local-optimums-in-e.tldr: Upper bounds on a run's eventual local optimum allow unpromising Gaussian-mixture EM runs to stop early.

paragraphs: Distributing expectation-maximization across machines is straightforward for part of the computation: given the parameters, individual data items can be processed independently in the E-step. Very large problems introduce another obstacle, however. The parameter collection itself may be too large to store on a single machine for the M-step, even when data processing has already been distributed.

This paper presents a framework that distributes the entire EM procedure. Each machine interacts only with parameters relevant to its own data. Machines coordinate by sending messages through a junction-tree topology, providing an organized structure for the communication needed to connect their local computations.

The framework targets a bottleneck that distributing the E-step alone does not address: central storage and handling of all parameters. The authors demonstrate improvements over a MapReduce approach on word alignment and topic modeling. These findings show the value of organizing both parameter access and computation across machines in the evaluated tasks, extending the scope of what distributed EM can practically handle.
icml-2008-fully-distributed-em-for-very-.tldr: A fully distributed EM framework spreads parameter handling across machines and improves on MapReduce in word alignment and topic modeling.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can require substantial memory and computation, making low-rank matrix approximations useful. The Nyström approach builds such an approximation using selected landmark points. This paper examines how the choice of those landmarks affects approximation quality, connecting the computational shortcut to how well the selected points summarize the data.

The authors derive an error analysis that directly relates approximation quality to the landmarks' ability to encode the dataset. The resulting bound suggests using k-means clustering as a simple, efficient way to obtain landmarks. This gives the selection procedure a theoretical motivation: a useful summary of the data can also support a useful approximation of the kernel matrix.

The proposed method is compared with leading alternatives, including greedy selection and probabilistic sampling. It achieves significant performance gains across several supervised and unsupervised tasks, including kernel PCA and least squares SVM. Together, the error analysis and experiments support paying attention to the representational quality of landmarks when reducing the cost of kernel-based learning.
icml-2008-improved-nystrom-low-rank-appr.tldr: An error bound motivates k-means landmark selection for Nyström approximation, with significant gains in several learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper addresses sparse learning for maximum margin Markov networks in structured prediction. The goal is to combine the maximum margin principle with a representation that uses parameters sparsely. The authors introduce the Laplace maximum margin Markov network, or LapM3N, as a model that provides this sparse representation.

LapM3N belongs to a broader family of Bayesian maximum margin Markov networks developed in the paper. That family rests on Structured Maximum Entropy Discrimination, a framework combining Bayesian learning and maximum margin learning for structured log-linear models. It also includes the existing unsparsified maximum margin Markov network as a special case, connecting the new formulation to an established approach.

For learning, the authors present an efficient iterative algorithm combining variational approximation with convex optimization methods already used for maximum margin Markov networks. Their method outperforms competing approaches on synthetic and real optical character recognition data. The contribution thus spans both modeling and computation: it supplies a framework for Bayesian margin-based learning, a sparse instance, and a practical training procedure.
icml-2008-laplace-maximum-margin-markov-.tldr: Laplace maximum margin Markov networks combine Bayesian and margin-based structured learning with sparse representations.

paragraphs: Listwise learning to rank treats an entire list as a training instance. A ranking function is learned by minimizing a loss that compares its predicted ordering with the ground-truth ordering. This paper investigates the theoretical foundations of that approach, addressing a gap left by earlier work that emphasized new algorithms and observed performance gains.

The analysis examines loss functions through properties including consistency, soundness, continuity, differentiability, convexity, and computational efficiency. The authors provide a sufficient condition for ranking consistency. Such a condition identifies circumstances under which consistency follows; it does not establish that the condition is required for every consistent ranking method.

The paper studies likelihood, cosine, and cross-entropy losses, with the latter two corresponding to RankCosine and ListNet. Using likelihood loss leads to a new method, ListMLE, whose loss offers better properties according to the analysis. Experiments support the theoretical results. The contribution is therefore both a way to assess ranking objectives and a new algorithm motivated by that assessment.
icml-2008-listwise-approach-to-learning-.tldr: The paper analyzes listwise ranking losses, gives a sufficient consistency condition, and introduces the likelihood-based ListMLE method.

paragraphs: This paper organizes several reinforcement learning algorithms into a generalized framework. It includes least-squares temporal difference learning, least-squares policy evaluation, and a variant of incremental least-squares temporal difference learning. Bringing these methods together provides a common way to describe algorithms that otherwise appear as separate procedures.

The framework is based on preconditioning while attempting to solve a stochastic model equation. Preconditioning changes how the equation is handled during computation, making it the central mechanism through which the paper relates and extends the included algorithms. The work also develops an iterative way to apply this mechanism, so the framework includes a concrete computational procedure.

Two further contributions address practical use. The authors introduce a step-size rule that can be computed online, allowing it to be determined during learning. They also reduce the complexity of related algorithms to near that of temporal difference learning. These results matter together: the framework connects existing methods while addressing the cost of applying preconditioning and selecting update sizes.
icml-2008-preconditioned-temporal-differ.tldr: A preconditioning framework unifies several temporal-difference methods and reduces related computational costs toward those of TD learning.

paragraphs: A retrieval system can return individually relevant results that repeat much of the same information. Diversity matters because a result set should cover different topics while using its limited space effectively. It is also useful when a query has multiple meanings, as with Jaguar referring to either a car or an animal.

This paper makes diversity an explicit training objective. The authors formulate retrieval as predicting a diverse subset and derive a training algorithm based on structural SVMs. Treating the subset as the prediction allows the learning problem to address the composition of the result set, including how its members collectively cover different topics.

The motivation has two parts: reduce redundancy and accommodate different interpretations of an ambiguous query. A broader selection gives more users a chance to find something relevant and presents more information within the returned results. The stated contribution is the learning formulation and its training algorithm, providing a direct way to train retrieval functions around diversity.
icml-2008-predicting-diverse-subsets-usi.tldr: The paper formulates diverse retrieval as subset prediction and derives a structural SVM algorithm that explicitly trains for diversity.

paragraphs: Physics-based simulations can describe complex systems in high detail, yet their computational cost can make systematic exploration difficult. An exhaustive grid with k settings along each of d input dimensions requires k to the power d trials. This rapid growth motivates choosing simulation inputs selectively, using previous results to guide what should be evaluated next.

The paper studies a directed exploration loop. Standard supervised learning methods, including SVMs, kernel density estimation, and Gaussian processes, build simplified predictive models from completed trials. An active learning procedure then uses those models to select valuable additional trials. The prediction model and the choice of new inputs are therefore linked throughout exploration.

The authors examine several selection strategies, including an information-theoretic approach. They evaluate performance using thirteen challenging oracles that stand in for more expensive simulations. These surrogates make the experiments easier for other researchers to replicate. The work provides a concrete setting for investigating how learned models can guide exploration when exhaustive simulation is prohibitively costly.
icml-2009-active-learning-for-directed-e.tldr: The paper studies active learning strategies that use predictive models to choose informative trials for exploring expensive simulated systems.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised classification uses labeled examples together with additional unlabeled data. A generative approach can make the unlabeled examples useful by modeling the data's probability density, helping reveal clusters that may assist classification. This paper addresses the difficulty of turning theoretically appealing nonparametric Bayesian models into practical methods for this setting.

The proposed model uses Gaussian processes for its generative component. The authors present this choice as avoiding many problems associated with Dirichlet process mixture models. The approach remains fully generative, so its treatment of classification is connected to a probability model of how the data arise.

Practical inference is supplied through recent advances in Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms. This is a central part of the contribution because a flexible probabilistic model must also support usable computation. Comparisons on synthetic and real-world multiclass data are favorable to the proposed method. The results support this combination of Gaussian-process generative modeling and sampling-based inference as a practical approach to semi-supervised learning.
icml-2009-archipelago-nonparametric-baye.tldr: Archipelago uses Gaussian-process generative modeling and practical Bayesian inference for semi-supervised multiclass classification.

paragraphs: This paper formalizes training strategies that organize examples in a meaningful progression, gradually introducing more concepts and greater complexity. It calls this curriculum learning. The key choice is the selection and order of training examples, making the training sequence itself part of the learning method.

The authors explore curricula in several settings, including the challenge of training deep deterministic and stochastic neural networks with nonconvex objectives. Their experiments show that a particular curriculum can produce significant improvements in generalization. This establishes that example ordering and selection can matter empirically, without implying that every easy-to-hard schedule will improve every learning problem.

The paper also proposes an explanation for these effects. The authors hypothesize that curricula can influence both convergence speed and the quality of the local minimum reached. They interpret curriculum learning as a form of continuation method, connecting gradual training to a broader strategy for nonconvex optimization. This interpretation is presented as a hypothesis about the mechanism underlying the observed benefits.
icml-2009-curriculum-learning-7198e7b6a5.tldr: Meaningfully ordering training examples can improve generalization, with hypothesized effects on optimization speed and the local minima reached.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a probability distribution over words from examples drawn independently from a fixed, unknown distribution. It focuses on rational stochastic languages, a class representable by multiplicity automata. These automata generalize probabilistic automata, giving the learning problem a particular algebraic structure.

For each prefix, consider the function that assigns a probability to every possible continuation after that prefix. In the target class, all these functions lie in a finite-dimensional vector space. This means that identifying the relevant space can serve as a first step toward learning the language distribution. The paper investigates principal component analysis as a way to perform that step.

The authors provide an inference algorithm that computes an estimate of the target distribution. They prove theoretical properties of the algorithm and report numerical simulations supporting the relevance of the approach. The central contribution is the connection between grammatical inference and subspace identification: a problem about probabilities of words can be approached through finite-dimensional linear structure.
icml-2009-grammatical-inference-as-a-pri.tldr: The paper uses finite-dimensional structure in rational stochastic languages to approach grammatical inference through principal component analysis.

paragraphs: Active learning seeks to learn from selectively requested labels, but selective sampling changes the data available to the learner. That sampling bias must be addressed if the resulting classifier is to reflect the underlying learning problem. This paper presents a practical, statistically consistent approach for binary classification under general loss functions.

The method uses importance weighting to correct the bias introduced by its sampling choices. It also controls variance, addressing the statistical variability associated with the weighted learning process. These two elements work together: the weighting corrects selection effects, while variance control enables rigorous bounds on the number of labels needed.

Experiments use passively labeled data to evaluate the approach. On many learning problems, it reduces the label requirements for obtaining good predictive performance. The contribution combines a practical method with statistical justification: selective labeling is paired with bias correction and label complexity guarantees. The empirical finding concerns reductions across many tested problems, rather than a claim that active selection always saves labels.
icml-2009-importance-weighted-active-lea.tldr: Importance weighting and variance control enable statistically consistent active learning with label complexity bounds and empirical label savings.

paragraphs: People using topic models may already know which words should receive high or low probability within particular topics. This paper provides a way to incorporate that knowledge into Latent Dirichlet Allocation. The goal is to let user knowledge influence the learned topics through the probabilistic model itself.

The authors introduce a Dirichlet forest prior, constructed as a mixture of specially structured Dirichlet tree distributions. The prior is the mechanism that expresses the supplied knowledge about topic composition. They describe how to construct it and perform inference using collapsed Gibbs sampling, connecting the knowledge representation to a concrete learning procedure.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the model can follow user-specified knowledge and generalize beyond it. That combination matters because useful guidance should influence learning while still allowing the data to support additional structure. The contribution is therefore a probabilistic route for combining explicit domain knowledge with topic discovery, accompanied by evidence that the resulting model can do more than reproduce the supplied guidance.
icml-2009-incorporating-domain-knowledge.tldr: A Dirichlet forest prior lets LDA incorporate user knowledge about word probabilities while learning beyond that guidance.

paragraphs: Interactive decision systems often assume that users describe preferences using a predefined catalog of features. This paper considers users who prefer to express themselves through different features, whose definitions in terms of the catalog are unknown. The system must therefore learn something about what the user's features mean while helping make a decision.

The authors formulate feature elicitation as concept learning. The objective is to identify enough about the unknown concepts to recommend a good alternative. This makes the information needed for the current decision central to learning, rather than requiring a complete definition of every user feature before a recommendation can be made.

The paper gives computational procedures for selecting alternatives according to minimax regret while concept uncertainty remains. This criterion addresses the worst-case shortfall associated with a choice under the remaining uncertainty. It also introduces heuristic query strategies aimed at reducing uncertainty that matters for the decision. Together, these components connect questions about feature meaning to the practical task of choosing an alternative.
icml-2009-online-feature-elicitation-in-.tldr: The paper learns enough about users' unfamiliar preference features to recommend alternatives using minimax regret.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose observations that distinguish competing models of a nonlinear dynamical system. Its approach selects an informative subset of time-dependent variables for Bayesian model inference. The decision concerns which observations are expected to help identify the model, making experimental selection part of the inference process.

The selection criterion maximizes expected Kullback-Leibler divergence between prior and posterior model probabilities. In plain language, it favors observations expected to change beliefs about the candidate models most informatively. The strategy generalizes standard D-optimal design, which arises under a uniform prior and Gaussian noise. It also provides an information-based criterion for halting model identification.

The authors illustrate the approach by distinguishing among eighteen published biochemical models of the TOR signaling pathway. In that model-selection problem, the strategy generates pivotal experiments and outperforms standard A-optimal, D-optimal, and E-optimal sequential design methods. The result supports directly optimizing expected information about model identity when deciding what to observe in this application.
icml-2009-optimized-expected-information.tldr: Selecting observations by expected information gain improves discrimination among eighteen biochemical models in the reported application.

paragraphs: This paper examines policy-gradient learning in partially observable Markov decision processes. It focuses on a class of policies based on predictive state representations and compares them with finite-state controllers, a standard policy representation in this setting. The central question is how the choice of representation affects the optimization problem faced during learning.

The authors introduce a general actor-critic algorithm for both representations. The critic computes a value function expressed in terms of the policy's parameters. Those parameters are then gradually updated to increase the value function. This gives the comparison a common learning framework rather than treating the two policy classes as unrelated algorithms.

The paper shows that the value function is polynomial for both classes, with potentially lower degree for predictive-state policies. Such policies can consequently have fewer local optima than equivalent finite-state controllers, making gradient learning more likely to reach a global optimum. The advantage is conditional: the argument identifies a possible improvement in the optimization landscape, not a guarantee of globally optimal learning.
icml-2009-predictive-representations-for.tldr: Predictive-state policies can yield simpler value-function landscapes than finite-state controllers, potentially improving policy-gradient optimization.

paragraphs: Dyadic data describe relationships between pairs of entities and appear in applications such as social network analysis and information retrieval. Topic models can uncover hidden structure in these relationships. This paper argues that probabilistic modeling should also account for the possibility that naturally occurring data lie on or near a lower-dimensional manifold.

The proposed framework models topical structure together with the data's geometry. It represents local manifold structure using a graph, then uses the graph Laplacian to smooth probability density functions. The Laplacian serves as a discrete counterpart to a manifold-based smoothing operator, connecting nearby data through the graph during probabilistic modeling.

As a result, the learned distributions concentrate around the data manifold. This matters because the model can reflect the local organization of the observations alongside their hidden topical structure. Experiments on real datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is the explicit integration of geometric information into probabilistic dyadic analysis, motivated by data whose structure may not be well represented by the surrounding Euclidean space alone.
icml-2009-probabilistic-dyadic-data-anal.tldr: Graph-based smoothing helps probabilistic models of dyadic data capture both hidden topics and local manifold structure.

paragraphs: Tree kernels compare tree-structured objects through their constituent structures. The paper identifies a gap in almost all earlier tree kernels: they match substructures without accounting for how those pieces are positioned relative to one another. This can leave relational information outside the comparison, even when the pieces themselves are recognized.

The authors propose a family of kernels based on routes between tree nodes. Routes make relative positioning an explicit part of the representation used to compare trees. They also provide an efficient implementation of one member of the family, connecting the proposed similarity measure to a computationally usable method.

Experiments on four datasets show that the method reaches state-of-the-art performance. In some cases it performs better than tree kernels that require more computation. These findings support including the arrangement of substructures when comparing trees, while also showing that the implemented route kernel can be computationally competitive. The empirical advantage is reported for some comparisons, rather than as uniform superiority over all tree kernels.
icml-2009-route-kernels-for-trees-34159b.tldr: Route-based tree kernels capture relative positioning and achieve competitive results with an efficient implementation.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes spectral clustering through the graph p-Laplacian, a nonlinear extension of the standard graph Laplacian. The parameter p changes the mathematical object used to derive a clustering. The authors investigate how this extension connects spectral methods to graph-cut objectives, giving the parameter a theoretical interpretation.

They show that the second eigenvector interpolates between a relaxation of the normalized cut and the Cheeger cut. More strongly, as p approaches one, thresholding that eigenvector produces a cut that converges to the optimal Cheeger cut. This is a limiting result tied to p approaching one, rather than a statement that every parameter choice immediately yields the optimal cut.

The paper also supplies an efficient numerical scheme for computing the second eigenvector. In the reported experiments, p-spectral clustering performs at least as well as ordinary spectral clustering and often significantly better. The work combines a theoretical connection to cut optimality with a computational method and empirical evidence that the generalized formulation can improve clustering.
icml-2009-spectral-clustering-based-on-t.tldr: Graph p-Laplacian clustering connects spectral methods to optimal Cheeger cuts in a limit and often improves experimental clustering results.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a deterministic method for approximating the integral of a positive function. Its central idea is to use smooth binning functions to divide the original integral into smaller pieces that are easier to approximate. These soft divisions allow the method to organize the calculation into local subproblems.

Each piece receives its own mean-field approximation. The resulting algorithm alternates between improving the bins and improving the approximations to the local integrals. Thus, the subdivision and the approximations are optimized together: the method adjusts how the integral is split as well as how each resulting part is evaluated.

The authors identify binning functions that allow an existing mean-field approximation to be extended into a split version without additional derivations. This makes the method useful as an extension of an established approximation procedure. They also explain its relationship to mixture mean-field methods, presenting it as a revival of related ideas. The contribution is a tractable construction for combining multiple local approximations within one integral calculation.
icml-2009-split-variational-inference-88.tldr: Split variational inference smoothly divides an integral into parts and jointly optimizes their bins and local mean-field approximations.

paragraphs: An inhomogeneous Poisson process models events whose intensity varies across time or space. Placing a Gaussian-process prior on that intensity yields a Gaussian Cox process, allowing Bayesian modeling of an unknown intensity function. The difficulty is computational: likelihood-based inference involves an intractable integral over an infinite-dimensional random function.

The paper introduces the Sigmoidal Gaussian Cox Process. Its generative formulation for Poisson data enables tractable inference through Markov chain Monte Carlo. The authors present it as the first approach to Gaussian Cox processes that supports inference without introducing approximations or replacing the function distribution with a finite-dimensional proxy.

This distinction concerns the model and inference construction: it avoids the approximations described in the abstract while still using a sampling-based inference method. The authors compare the approach with competing methods on synthetic data and apply it to several real-world datasets. The contribution makes this flexible class of event-intensity models computationally accessible through a generative construction designed around the inference obstacle.
icml-2009-tractable-nonparametric-bayesi.tldr: The Sigmoidal Gaussian Cox Process enables tractable MCMC inference without the model approximations or finite-dimensional proxies described in the abstract.
